cards.text: Paul has just been through a city-wide uproar, and now it's finally over. He's about to head out. But before he goes, he sends for the disciples.

cards.question: Paul sends for the disciples one more time before he leaves. What does he do with them?

answers.text: He scolds them for the riot

cards.text: He says goodbye and leaves for Macedonia, speaking many words of encouragement all through that area. Then he arrives in Greece.

cards.question: Paul stays in Greece for three ___.

cards.text: Paul's about to sail for Syria when some Jews form a plot against him. People cancel their trips over this kind of thing all the time. I had MY travel plans cancelled for years, and I lived in a drawer!

cards.question: With a plot against him right as he's about to sail for Syria, what does Paul decide to do?

cards.text: Paul's not traveling alone, either. Seven men go with him, from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and the province of Asia, and one of them is Timothy.
Those men go on ahead and wait in Troas. And catch this: the writer says they waited for "us." Whoever's writing this story just joined the trip.

cards.question: Paul and the writer sail from Philippi to catch up with the others in Troas. After which feast do they set sail?
After sailing from Philippi, they rejoin the others in Troas five days later.

cards.text: They stay in Troas seven days. Then on the first day of the week, everyone comes together to break bread, and Paul's got one last night with them.

cards.question: Paul is ready to leave the next day, so he talks to them and keeps on speaking until ___.

cards.text: The upper room where they're gathered is full of lamps. And a young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window while Paul talks on and on.

cards.question: As Paul talks on and on, Eutychus sinks into a deep sleep.

cards.text: Friend, I can't judge. I once dozed off waiting on ONE batch of cookies. Twelve minutes. But Eutychus is sound asleep, and then... he falls from the third story.

cards.question: When they pick Eutychus up after his fall from the third story, he's shaken up but fine.

cards.text: But Paul goes down, throws himself on the young man and wraps him up in a hug.

cards.question: Paul tells everyone not to be alarmed. He says the young man is still ___.
A young man just fell out of a WINDOW. I'd need a week off. Paul goes back upstairs, breaks bread and eats. Then what does he do?

answers.text: Leaves for the ship right away

cards.text: At daybreak Paul heads out, and the people are greatly relieved to take the boy home alive. Paul's still on the road, friend, and this journey isn't done yet.

findings.problem: The passage starts in the middle of a thought: 'When the uproar had ended.' The opening card never says where Paul is (Ephesus) or what the uproar was, so the baker has no context for it.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: 'City-wide uproar' is a fact from Acts 19 (the city filled with confusion, Acts 19:29). Acts 20:1 says only 'the uproar.' The card states the outside fact without its reference.

rule.text: References. Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke fails the logic test. Paul's core action is rerouting his trip to get away from a plot. Being stuck in a drawer for years is a different action. 'People cancel their trips over this kind of thing all the time' (a plot against them) doesn't click for an adult, so a stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The setup line 'People cancel their trips over this kind of thing' tells the baker Paul changes his plans. That rules out the wrong answer 'Sail for Syria anyway' on card 6.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Timothy appears here for the first time in the lesson, but the card never says who he is.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The card says all seven men come from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and the province of Asia. Acts 20:4 gives no hometown for Timothy, so the card fills in something the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: 'Whoever's writing this story just joined the trip' isn't something the text shows. The 'we/us' wording already appeared earlier in Acts (Acts 16:10-17). Acts 20:5 says only that the men waited for 'us.'

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: Whether the trip took five days can only be answered by luck. Cards 4, 9 and 12 are also discovery questions, so this card adds another pure-guess number detail that doesn't move the passage forward.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Card 11's setup, 'Paul's got one last night with them,' rules out 'sunset' and 'noon,' which leaves 'midnight' as the only believable answer.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'Full of lamps' stretches the text. Acts 20:8 says there were 'many lamps.'

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: No card ever says Eutychus was picked up dead (Acts 20:9). The true or false card only shows he wasn't 'fine,' so the baker can leave without the key detail that makes verse 10 a raising.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'asleep' is true elsewhere in the passage: Eutychus was 'sound asleep' (Acts 20:9). With 'still,' a baker could argue 'still asleep' is right.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: Most cards are plain narration in a pleasant-dad tone. Only cards 5, 15 and 19 try a joke, and card 5's doesn't land. Moments that can hold a real laugh, like Paul talking until midnight (card 11) or 'on and on' (card 13), are passed over.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
